title: Deleted items are distinguished from temporarily unavailable items in availability responses
gherkin:
Feature: Availability State Semantics Separation
  Scenario: Deleted items have distinct lifecycle handling
    Given an item exists in the system
    When the item is deleted
    Then the availability query response must indicate the item is operationally invalid
    And the response must distinguish deletion from temporary unavailability states
    And the response must not use the same wording as temporarily blocked items
rationale: E5 confirms that current implementation conflates deleted items with temporarily blocked items in query responses, causing user confusion about recoverability. This test ensures deleted items are semantically separated with distinct lifecycle handling as specified in the operative context.
usedContextItems: System must distinguish between different non-rentable states (deleted items, maintenance periods, manual restrictions, temporary unavailability)|Deleted items should have distinct lifecycle handling separate from temporary non-rentable states|Availability query API must clearly communicate the reason or category of unavailability to prevent user confusion about item recoverability
generationSummary: R50 requires semantic separation of availability states to distinguish between operationally invalid items (deleted) and temporarily unavailable items (maintenance, manual blocks, active rentals). Tests validate that the system correctly categorizes and communicates different non-rentable states, prevents user confusion about item recoverability, and ensures availability semantics reflect operational validity separately from temporary unavailability.
resolvedOperativeContext: System must distinguish between different non-rentable states (deleted items, maintenance periods, manual restrictions, temporary unavailability) in availability semantics and query responses || Availability state semantics must separate operational validity (whether an item exists and is managed) from temporary unavailability (maintenance, manual blocks, active rentals) || Availability query API must clearly communicate the reason or category of unavailability to prevent user confusion about item recoverability || Item availability status must be immediately updated when rental lifecycle events or availability controls change
resolvedExceptions: Items marked Unavailable through status toggle cannot be rented || Manual availability restrictions take precedence over otherwise rentable time windows || Maintenance periods block rental activity and make items appear non-rentable during the maintenance window || Deleted items should have distinct lifecycle handling separate from temporary non-rentable states
resolvedConflictsOrObsolete: Availability query results surface operationally invalid records using the same wording as temporarily blocked items, misleading users about recoverability (E5) || Implementation path uses existing non-rentable status handling for maintenance without confirming whether UI distinction is required (E6) || Earlier discussion suggested single fallback delay after rental events, but current availability rules do not support uniform timing assumptions (E2)
resolutionNotes: R50 targets semantic separation of availability states to resolve ambiguity between operationally invalid items (deleted) and temporarily unavailable items (maintenance, manual blocks, active rentals). Primary evidence (E5, E6) confirms that current implementation conflates these categories in query responses, causing user confusion. E13 provides the baseline availability specification (TOOLCHAIN-CONF-AVAILABILITY-01) defining calculation, query, and restriction rules. E14 and E15 reference related requirements on query correctness and deleted-vs-unavailable ambiguity. The core operative rule is that availability semantics must distinguish state categories to enable accurate user communication about item recoverability. Gaps remain on deleted-item mapping, UI distinction requirements, and category-dependent timing details.
